newsitem.title: CHINA: Rival Koreas sign accord on food for hungry North.
newsitem.headline: Rival Koreas sign accord on food for hungry North.

text.p: Seoul on Monday agreed to send thousands of tonnes of food aid to Pyongyang under the first direct agreement between the Red Cross societies of rival North and South Korea in more than a decade.

"We have no doubt that this agreement will (help build momentum) to increase mutual cooperation between (the) two Koreas on the basis of humanitarianism," said South Korean Red Cross official Kogh Young-kee.
Under the accord, South Korea would ship 50,000 tonnes of food aid to its famine-threatened Stalinist neighbour by the end of July, Kogh told reporters after the signing ceremony in a Beijing hotel.
The accord was the first between the Red Cross societies of the Cold War rivals since a 1985 pact on hometown visits by displaced families, Kogh said.

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean civil war ended only in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made even basic food aid a delicate diplomatic affair.

Despite the increasingly desperate situation in North Korea, which is suffering widespread hunger after years of economic malaise and natural disasters, Pyongyang has retained strict controls on contacts with its prosperous neighbour.

Corn would account for most of the 50,000 tonnes of food promised by Seoul as the first stage of direct Red Cross assistance, but wheat, milk powder and instant noodles would also be donated, South Korean officials said.

Under the accord, which was reached after three days of often difficult talks in Beijing, the aid would be transported through two ports in North Korea and also by land across the isolated nation's border with China.
Seoul officials said they were disappointed that Pyongyang had not accepted shipments through the town of Panmunjom, which straddles the militarised border between the two Koreas.
"We are very disappointed not to send through Panmunjom ... Because most of our people want to use the Panmunjom area," said one official after the signing ceremony.
Seoul had argued that the Panmunjom route was the most direct and cost-effective and that shipping through China meant extra delays getting the food to hungry Northern compatriots.

North Korea, which takes self-reliance as its guiding ideology, has sought to limit any direct contact involved in taking grain from the South, while Seoul wants to maximise exchanges and to make sure its aid is clearly labelled as South Korean.
Pyongyang had accepted that commercial products would retain their labelled packets during distribution and that other food aid would have Red Cross and donor identification, said Kogh.
Inter-Korean talks in Beijing earlier this month failed after South Korea declined to say how much aid it would supply. Seoul later promised to ship food worth $8 million.

Seoul officials said agreement in the latest round of Beijing talks was delayed by Pyongyang's demands for a larger food package as well as by differences over how to transport, package and distribute it.

While Monday's pledge of 50,000 tonnes of food is dwarfed by aid promised by other donors -- the European Commission said last Friday it was sending 155,000 tonnes -- it is expected to lead to further shipments from the prosperous South.
